conflicts.name: The Boxer Uprising and the Allied intervention
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Hostility to Christianity was at the heart of the Boxer movement: its placards blamed missionaries and converts for drought and disorder, and Chinese Christians were by far its most numerous victims. Yet historians such as Joseph Esherick and Paul Cohen stress that the anti-Christian violence grew out of a wider crisis — foreign imperial pressure, the legal privileges missionaries won for converts, village feuds, and a catastrophic drought in north China — and that the Qing court backed the Boxers for dynastic and anti-foreign rather than religious reasons. On the Allied side religion was not a war aim, though missionaries supplied grievances, guides and indemnity claims, and some Western rhetoric framed the relief of the legations as the rescue of Christian civilisation. Religion is therefore best described as a major, not the sole, driver.

sides.name: Boxers (Yihequan, ‘Righteous and Harmonious Fists’) and, from June 1900, the Qing court
sides.faith: Chinese popular religion: spirit-possession martial arts, Daoist and Buddhist deities, heroes of popular opera

sides.name: Eight-Nation Alliance (Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, United States, Italy, Austria-Hungary)
sides.faith: Christian-majority powers (and Shinto/Buddhist Japan) with no religious war aim
leaders: Sir Claude MacDonald (British minister in Beijing)

sides.name: Chinese Christians, missionaries and besieged foreigners
leaders: Protestant missionary communities in the Legation Quarter

conflicts.summary: A popular movement of north Chinese villagers, the Boxers, attacked missionaries and above all Chinese Christian converts in 1899–1900, blaming them for drought and foreign encroachment. When the Qing court declared war on the foreign powers in June 1900, the Beijing legations and the Catholic Beitang cathedral were besieged until an eight-nation army relieved them in August; Allied punitive expeditions and looting followed, and the 1901 Boxer Protocol imposed a vast indemnity on China. Some 30,000 Chinese Catholics, around 2,000 Chinese Protestants and roughly 200 foreign missionaries and their children were killed.
conflicts.story:
By the 1890s Christianity in China was entangled with foreign power. The ‘unequal treaties’ after the Opium Wars and the Tianjin and Beijing conventions of 1858–60 protected missionaries and allowed them to buy property in the interior; France claimed a protectorate over Catholic missions, and missionaries frequently intervened with magistrates on behalf of converts in lawsuits. To many villagers, converts appeared to be a privileged community that refused to contribute to temple festivals and could call on foreign gunboats. ‘Missionary cases’ (jiao’an) — riots, disputed property and lawsuits — multiplied, especially in Shandong. When two German Catholic missionaries were murdered at Juye in November 1897, Germany used the incident to seize Jiaozhou Bay, deepening the identification of mission with conquest.

The Boxers emerged in western Shandong in 1898–99 among poor peasants hit by Yellow River floods and then a severe drought. They practised martial-arts rituals in which young men were possessed by gods drawn from popular novels and opera and believed themselves invulnerable to bullets; girls’ groups, the Red Lanterns, claimed comparable powers. Their placards declared that rain would not fall until the foreigners and their ‘secondary devils’ — the converts — were destroyed, and their slogan became ‘Support the Qing, destroy the foreign’ (fu Qing mie yang). The killing of the English missionary Sidney Brooks on 31 December 1899 was the first death of a foreign missionary, but from the start most of those killed were Chinese Christians.

In spring 1900 the movement spread across the drought-stricken plains of Zhili towards Beijing and Tianjin, burning churches, railway stations and telegraph lines. Factions at court, led by Prince Duan and supported by the Empress Dowager Cixi, saw the Boxers as a loyal militia against foreign aggression. A first relief column under the British admiral Edward Seymour was turned back in mid-June; the Allies stormed the Dagu (Taku) forts on 17 June; on 20 June the German minister Clemens von Ketteler was shot in the street, and on 21 June the court declared war on the foreign powers. For fifty-five days some 900 foreigners and around 3,000 Chinese Christians held out in the Legation Quarter, while about 3,400 Catholics, with French and Italian marines, defended the Beitang (Northern) cathedral under Bishop Alphonse Favier.

The worst massacres took place in the provinces. At Baoding at the end of June and start of July American Presbyterian and Congregational missionaries were killed; at Taiyuan on 9 July the governor of Shanxi, Yuxian, had some forty-four foreign Protestants and Catholics, including women and children, executed in his yamen, and many more Chinese Christians were killed across Shanxi, Zhili and Inner Mongolia. Some converts renounced their faith to save their lives; many were killed in whole families. Southern governors-general, notably Li Hongzhang, Zhang Zhidong and Liu Kunyi, ignored the declaration of war and protected foreigners in the ‘Mutual Protection of the Southeast’, limiting the war to the north.

A second, larger Allied army of about 20,000 men marched from Tianjin in early August and relieved the legations on 14 August; Cixi and the emperor fled to Xi’an. What followed was itself an atrocity: Beijing was systematically looted, by soldiers, diplomats and some missionaries, and German-led punitive expeditions under Field Marshal von Waldersee burned villages suspected of Boxer sympathy and executed suspects with little or no trial. Kaiser Wilhelm II had told his departing troops at Bremerhaven on 27 July to give no quarter and make the name of Germany feared ‘like the Huns’. On the Amur, Russian forces drove thousands of Chinese residents of Blagoveshchensk into the river to drown in July 1900, and Russia occupied Manchuria.

The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 ordered the execution or suicide of senior officials, including Yuxian, permanent foreign garrisons in the capital and an indemnity of 450 million taels payable over thirty-nine years. Missions also negotiated local compensation for destroyed property and murdered converts, sometimes extracting fines from whole villages. The American Board missionary William Scott Ament’s collection of such indemnities was publicly attacked by Mark Twain in ‘To the Person Sitting in Darkness’ (1901), while Hudson Taylor’s China Inland Mission declined compensation for its own losses.

The aftermath reshaped both China and the missions. The Qing undertook late reforms but fell in 1911; Chinese nationalists of the 1920s, in the anti-Christian movement, recalled 1900 as proof that Christianity was the vanguard of imperialism, while churches commemorated the dead as martyrs. Missions grew rapidly in the following decades, and part of the American share of the indemnity was remitted from 1908 to fund Chinese students, leading to Tsinghua University. In 2000 Pope John Paul II canonised 120 Martyrs of China, among them many Catholics killed in 1900 — a canonisation, held on 1 October, China’s National Day, that the People’s Republic denounced as a glorification of imperialism.
conflicts.nameOfGod: On the Boxer side the divine was invoked through popular religion: possessing deities such as Guan Yu and the Monkey King, charms and incantations that promised invulnerability, and placards announcing that heaven withheld rain because of the foreign religion. On the Christian side, missionaries and converts interpreted the killings as martyrdom and the defence of the Beitang as divine deliverance; Western propaganda and some sermons cast the relief of the legations as the defence of Christian civilisation against heathen barbarism, and missionaries such as Ament defended punitive indemnities as just retribution.
religiousCauses: Boxer ideology blamed the Christian religion for offending the gods, causing the drought and disrupting village harmony, and its placards called for killing missionaries and converts.
Converts’ refusal to contribute to temple festivals and opera performances made them appear as dissenters from village religious life.
Missionary intervention in lawsuits on behalf of converts, and French claims to protect Catholics, created resentment of Christians as a protected caste.
Rumours about missions — that orphanages killed children for their eyes and hearts, and that churches practised sorcery — were spread in anti-Christian tracts since the 1860s.
Disputes over church property, including the return of old Catholic sites under the 1860 Beijing Convention, turned temples and land into flashpoints.
otherCauses: The ‘scramble for concessions’ of 1897–98, including the German seizure of Jiaozhou Bay and Russian, British and French leases, created fear that China would be partitioned.
Yellow River floods in 1898 and severe drought in 1899–1900 left young men idle and hungry across Shandong and Zhili.
Railways, telegraphs and imported goods disrupted the carting, boat and handicraft trades on which many depended.
Court politics after the failed Hundred Days’ Reform of 1898 strengthened conservative, anti-foreign princes around Cixi.
A tradition of martial-arts societies and anti-dynastic sects in north China supplied networks and rituals.
triggers: The murder of two German Catholic missionaries at Juye in November 1897 and Germany’s seizure of Jiaozhou Bay in response.
The spread of Boxer bands from Shandong into Zhili in spring 1900 during drought.
The Allied attack on the Dagu forts on 17 June 1900 and the shooting of the German minister von Ketteler on 20 June.
The Qing court’s declaration of war on the foreign powers on 21 June 1900.

timeline.text: Two German missionaries of the Society of the Divine Word are killed at Juye, Shandong; Germany seizes Jiaozhou Bay.
Yellow River floods devastate Shandong; the Hundred Days’ Reform ends in Cixi’s coup.
Boxer groups clash with converts in north-west Shandong; the Anglican missionary Sidney Brooks is killed on 31 December.
June: Boxers enter Beijing and Tianjin; the Seymour expedition is turned back; the Dagu forts fall; von Ketteler is killed; the court declares war (21 June).
June–August: siege of the Legation Quarter and the Beitang cathedral; massacres of missionaries and converts at Baoding and Taiyuan (9 July).
July: Russian forces drown thousands of Chinese at Blagoveshchensk; Wilhelm II’s ‘Hun speech’ at Bremerhaven (27 July).
14 August: the eight-nation relief force enters Beijing; Cixi flees to Xi’an; looting and punitive expeditions follow.
7 September: the Boxer Protocol imposes an indemnity of 450 million taels and executions of officials.
Shanxi University is founded with Shanxi indemnity funds at Timothy Richard’s proposal; Cixi returns to Beijing.
The United States begins remitting part of its indemnity to fund Chinese students.
Pope John Paul II canonises 120 Martyrs of China, many of them killed in 1900.

keyPeople.name: Empress Dowager Cixi
keyPeople.role: Effective ruler of the Qing dynasty
keyPeople.focus: Allowed the Boxers into the capital and sanctioned the declaration of war on the powers in June 1900, then fled to Xi’an.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned in 1902, blamed subordinates, and presided over the late Qing reforms until her death in 1908.

keyPeople.name: Yuxian
keyPeople.role: Governor of Shandong, then of Shanxi
keyPeople.focus: Patronised the Boxers and ordered the execution of foreign missionaries and their families at Taiyuan on 9 July 1900.
keyPeople.outcome: Executed in 1901 at the Allies’ demand under the Boxer Protocol.

keyPeople.name: Alphonse Favier
keyPeople.focus: Directed the defence of the Beitang cathedral, where thousands of Chinese Catholics endured a two-month siege.
keyPeople.outcome: Survived; later criticised for his part in post-war reprisals and compensation claims.

keyPeople.name: James Hudson Taylor
keyPeople.role: Founder of the China Inland Mission
keyPeople.focus: His mission lost more members than any other — 58 adults and 21 children; he directed that no compensation be demanded.
keyPeople.outcome: The refusal was widely noted in China; he retired soon afterwards and died at Changsha in 1905.

keyPeople.name: Timothy Richard
keyPeople.focus: Negotiated a Shanxi settlement in which indemnity money funded a modern university rather than punishment.
keyPeople.outcome: Shanxi University opened in 1902; he is remembered as a reformist voice within missions.

keyPeople.name: William Scott Ament
keyPeople.focus: Led armed parties collecting indemnities and goods from villages for murdered converts after the relief.
keyPeople.outcome: Satirised by Mark Twain in 1901, he became a symbol of missionary complicity in reprisals.

keyPeople.name: Alfred von Waldersee
keyPeople.focus: Arrived after the relief and directed dozens of punitive expeditions into the countryside in 1900–01.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned to Germany in 1901; the expeditions became notorious for summary executions.

keyPeople.name: Li Hongzhang
keyPeople.focus: Kept south China out of the war and negotiated the Boxer Protocol.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in November 1901, weeks after signing it.

casualties.note: The best-documented figures concern Christians: roughly 30,000 Chinese Catholics and about 2,000 Chinese Protestants were killed, together with some 200 foreign missionaries and their children (about 136 Protestant adults and 53 children, and over 40 Catholic priests, brothers and sisters). Allied military deaths were about 2,500. The number of Boxers, Qing soldiers and Chinese civilians killed in fighting, at Blagoveshchensk and in Allied punitive expeditions was never counted; total estimates of 100,000 or more are common but rest on little systematic evidence.

effects: The Boxer Protocol of 1901 burdened the Qing with a 450-million-tael indemnity and foreign garrisons, hastening the dynasty’s collapse in 1911.
Russia occupied Manchuria, a step towards the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05.
The court turned to the New Policies reforms, including the abolition of the civil-service examinations in 1905.
The episode fixed in Western culture the image of the ‘Yellow Peril’, and in Chinese nationalism the image of imperialist looting and humiliation.
Remitted American and British indemnity funds paid for Chinese students abroad and institutions such as Tsinghua University.
effectsOnChurch: Catholic and Protestant churches commemorated thousands of martyrs; the 2000 canonisation of the Martyrs of China made 1900 central to Catholic memory and sharpened tension with Beijing.
Missions expanded rapidly after 1901, with more schools, hospitals and universities, partly as a deliberate response to the uprising.
Missionary participation in looting and indemnity collection discredited missions in Chinese eyes and fed the 1920s anti-Christian movement.
Some missionaries and Chinese Christian leaders drew the lesson that churches must be self-governing and detached from foreign power, a theme later taken up in indigenous and Three-Self movements.
Local Christian communities, especially in Shanxi and Zhili, were left with enduring divisions between families who had apostatised and those who had suffered.
conflicts.legacy: The Boxer Uprising remains contested in memory. For decades after 1949 Chinese historiography celebrated it as patriotic anti-imperialism; since the 1980s scholars have also stressed its superstition and cruelty towards fellow Chinese. For the churches it is both a story of martyrdom and an uncomfortable example of how closely mission had become bound to gunboats, treaties and indemnities.

dissenters.name: James Hudson Taylor and the China Inland Mission
dissenters.text: Although the CIM suffered the heaviest losses, Taylor and the mission refused to claim indemnity for their own losses, arguing that Christians should not exact payment for suffering endured for Christ.

dissenters.name: Timothy Richard
dissenters.text: The Welsh Baptist argued against punitive fines and proposed instead that Shanxi’s indemnity fund a modern university to educate Chinese students.

dissenters.name: Critics of the looting within the missionary and church press
dissenters.text: Several missionaries and church newspapers in Britain and the United States condemned the participation of missionaries in looting and punitive raids as a betrayal of the gospel.

campaigns.title: The Seymour expedition
campaigns.people: About 2,000 sailors and marines of eight nations under Admiral Edward Seymour
campaigns.text: Setting out by rail on 10 June 1900 to relieve the legations, the column was blocked by Boxers and Qing troops near Langfang, retreated along the Hai River and was itself rescued at the Xigu Arsenal on 25 June.

campaigns.title: The relief of the Beijing legations
campaigns.people: About 20,000 Japanese, Russian, British, American and French troops; British commander Alfred Gaselee
campaigns.text: Leaving Tianjin on 4 August, the allied army defeated Qing forces at Beicang and Yangcun, reached Tongzhou on 12 August and broke into Beijing on 14 August; the Beitang was relieved two days later.

campaigns.title: The flight of the court to Xi’an
campaigns.people: Empress Dowager Cixi, the Guangxu Emperor and the court
campaigns.text: Disguised as commoners, Cixi and the emperor left Beijing on 15 August 1900 and travelled through Shanxi to Xi’an, returning in January 1902 after the Protocol was signed.

conflicts.name: The Cristero War in Mexico
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Religion was both the stated and the real cause: the rising followed the bishops’ suspension of public worship in protest at the enforcement of the 1917 Constitution’s anticlerical articles, and the rebels fought under the cry ‘¡Viva Cristo Rey!’. Jean Meyer’s pioneering work, based on interviews with veterans, presented the Cristiada as a genuine popular religious war of peasants defending their sacraments. Later regional studies (Matthew Butler, Jennie Purnell) add that land reform, local factional rivalries, hostility to agrarista communities and resistance to state centralisation shaped who joined and who fought against them — and that many devout Catholics did not rebel. The government, for its part, presented the war as a struggle of the Revolution against clerical reaction.

sides.name: Cristeros (Liga Nacional Defensora de la Libertad Religiosa and rural Catholic insurgents)
Federal government of Mexico, army and agrarista militias
sides.faith: Revolutionary secular state (anticlerical; many soldiers were themselves nominally Catholic)

conflicts.summary: When President Plutarco Elías Calles enforced the anticlerical articles of the 1917 Constitution in 1926, the Mexican bishops suspended public worship and tens of thousands of Catholic peasants in west-central Mexico rose in arms under the cry ‘¡Viva Cristo Rey!’. Three years of guerrilla war, executions of priests and rebels, reprisals against villages and attacks on government teachers and trains ended in the ‘arreglos’ of June 1929, a compromise negotiated by the bishops and the government with American mediation.
conflicts.story:
The Mexican Revolution’s Constitution of 1917 sought to break the Church’s social and political power. Article 3 secularised education, Article 5 banned monastic vows, Article 24 confined worship to church buildings under state supervision, Article 27 nationalised church property, and Article 130 denied the Church legal personality, barred foreign-born priests, forbade clergy to criticise the laws or vote, and allowed states to limit the number of priests. Under Álvaro Obregón these provisions were applied unevenly, but Catholic social and lay movements, especially in Jalisco under Anacleto González Flores’ Unión Popular, grew in strength, and in 1925 the government sponsored a schismatic ‘Mexican Catholic Apostolic Church’.

Plutarco Elías Calles, president from 1924, was determined to enforce the Constitution. The ‘Calles Law’ of June 1926 reformed the penal code to punish violations with fines and imprisonment, ordered the registration of priests and expelled foreign clergy. With the approval of Pope Pius XI, the Mexican bishops responded by suspending all public worship from 31 July 1926 — for the first time since the Spanish conquest no Mass was publicly celebrated in Mexico. The Liga Nacional Defensora de la Libertad Religiosa (founded 1925) organised an economic boycott and a petition of some two million signatures, which Congress rejected.

Scattered risings broke out in August 1926, and from January 1927 the Liga called for a general insurrection. Its urban leaders expected a quick victory; instead the war was carried by rural people, often smallholders and ranchers in Jalisco, Michoacán, Colima, Guanajuato, Zacatecas and Nayarit, who fought for the restoration of the sacraments. Anacleto González Flores, who had long advocated non-violent resistance, accepted leadership of the rising in Jalisco; he was captured, tortured and shot in Guadalajara on 1 April 1927. Three weeks later a Cristero band led by Fr José Reyes Vega attacked the Guadalajara–Mexico City train near La Barca, and many civilian passengers died when carriages were set alight, an atrocity the government used to justify the mass expulsion of bishops.

The federal army under Joaquín Amaro answered with ‘reconcentration’ of the rural population of Los Altos into towns, scorched-earth sweeps, the hanging of suspected rebels along railway lines and the execution of priests found exercising ministry, many of whom the Catholic Church later canonised. In Mexico City the Jesuit Miguel Agustín Pro was shot without trial on 23 November 1927 after a bomb attack on Obregón, a death photographed by the government. Cristeros in turn killed agraristas, government officials and rural schoolteachers of the new secular schools, some of whom were mutilated. From 1927 the Cristero forces were reorganised by a professional soldier, Enrique Gorostieta, a liberal sceptic hired by the Liga, and by 1929 perhaps 50,000 men were under arms.

Politics shifted in 1928, when the president-elect Obregón was assassinated on 17 July by José de León Toral, a young Catholic militant; the nun Concepción Acevedo de la Llata (‘Madre Conchita’) was convicted as an accomplice. The Escobar rebellion of March 1929 strained the army, but Cristero victories, such as at Tepatitlán in April 1929, could not take cities. Gorostieta was killed in an ambush near Atotonilco on 2 June 1929.

The American ambassador Dwight Morrow and the Paulist priest John J. Burke brokered talks between President Emilio Portes Gil and two bishops, Leopoldo Ruiz y Flores and Pascual Díaz Barreto. The ‘arreglos’ (arrangements) of 21 June 1929 left the Constitution unchanged but promised that registration would not be used to destroy the Church’s hierarchy, that religious instruction could be given in churches, and that rebels would be amnestied. Bells rang and worship resumed on 30 June. Many Cristeros felt betrayed by bishops who had never been fully united behind the war, and in the following years hundreds of former rebel leaders were killed despite the amnesty.

Persecution revived in the 1930s with ‘socialist education’, a second, smaller rising (La Segunda, 1934–38) and Pius XI’s encyclicals Acerba animi (1932) and Firmissimam constantiam (1937). Tensions eased under Lázaro Cárdenas and Manuel Ávila Camacho, who declared ‘soy creyente’ in 1940, and relations were fully normalised only in 1992, when Mexico amended the Constitution and established diplomatic relations with the Holy See. The war also drove tens of thousands of Mexicans to emigrate to the United States.
conflicts.nameOfGod: The rebels’ cry was ‘¡Viva Cristo Rey y Santa María de Guadalupe!’, echoing Pius XI’s feast of Christ the King instituted in 1925. Cristeros carried banners of the Virgin of Guadalupe, wore scapulars, received sacraments from priests in the field and saw death in battle as martyrdom. Some bishops, notably José de Jesús Manríquez y Zárate of Huejutla, defended armed resistance as legitimate under traditional teaching on resistance to tyranny, while the episcopate as a body never formally endorsed the rising. The government in turn branded its enemies ‘fanatics’ and defended the war as the defence of the secular Revolution.
religiousCauses: The anticlerical articles of the 1917 Constitution restricted worship, banned religious orders and denied the Church legal standing.
The Calles Law of 1926 made these provisions enforceable with criminal penalties and required the registration of priests.
The bishops’ suspension of public worship from 31 July 1926 deprived Catholic communities of Mass, baptism and marriage in church.
A vigorous Catholic lay movement shaped by Rerum Novarum and the cult of Christ the King gave Catholics organisations and a language of resistance.
The government’s sponsorship of a schismatic national church in 1925 was seen as an attack on the Church’s unity.
otherCauses: Agrarian reform set landless agraristas, armed by the state, against smallholders and ranchers in regions such as Los Altos.
Resistance to a centralising post-revolutionary state, its tax collectors and its schoolteachers ran deep in rural western Mexico.
Local feuds and factional rivalries determined which villages rebelled and which supported the government.
Calles’s political project of building a modern, secular national identity regarded the Church as its chief rival.
triggers: The Calles Law of 14 June 1926, which took effect on 31 July 1926.
The suspension of public worship by the bishops on 31 July 1926.
The Congress’s rejection of the Catholic petition in September 1926 and the Liga’s call to arms for January 1927.

timeline.text: The Querétaro Constitution includes sweeping anticlerical articles (3, 5, 24, 27, 130).
Founding of the Liga Nacional Defensora de la Libertad Religiosa; Pius XI institutes the feast of Christ the King.
The Calles Law is promulgated; the bishops suspend public worship on 31 July; Pius XI protests in Iniquis afflictisque (18 November).
General rising in January; Anacleto González Flores executed (1 April); La Barca train attack (April); Miguel Pro shot (23 November).
President-elect Álvaro Obregón is assassinated by the Catholic militant José de León Toral (17 July).
Cristero victory at Tepatitlán (April); Gorostieta killed (2 June); the arreglos are signed (21 June) and worship resumes.
‘Socialist education’ provokes a second, smaller Cristero rising, La Segunda (to 1938).
Miguel Pro is beatified by Pope John Paul II.
Constitutional reform recognises churches’ legal status; Mexico and the Holy See establish diplomatic relations.
John Paul II canonises 25 martyrs of the persecution, including Cristóbal Magallanes.
José Sánchez del Río, a boy Cristero killed in 1928, is canonised by Pope Francis.

keyPeople.name: Plutarco Elías Calles
keyPeople.role: President of Mexico 1924–28 and ‘Jefe Máximo’ thereafter
keyPeople.focus: Enforced the constitutional restrictions on the Church and directed the war against the Cristeros.
keyPeople.outcome: Dominated politics until exiled by Lázaro Cárdenas in 1936; returned to Mexico in 1941.

keyPeople.name: Anacleto González Flores
keyPeople.role: Lawyer and leader of the Catholic Unión Popular
keyPeople.focus: Organised non-violent resistance and the boycott, then reluctantly endorsed the armed rising in Jalisco.
keyPeople.outcome: Tortured and shot in Guadalajara on 1 April 1927; beatified in 2005.

keyPeople.name: Enrique Gorostieta Velarde
keyPeople.focus: A professional soldier hired by the Liga, he turned scattered bands into a disciplined guerrilla force.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed in an ambush near Atotonilco el Alto on 2 June 1929, weeks before the peace.

keyPeople.name: Miguel Agustín Pro
keyPeople.focus: Ministered clandestinely in Mexico City; arrested after a bomb attack on Obregón in which he had no part.
keyPeople.outcome: Executed without trial on 23 November 1927, crying ‘¡Viva Cristo Rey!’; beatified in 1988.

keyPeople.name: José de León Toral
keyPeople.focus: Assassinated president-elect Álvaro Obregón on 17 July 1928.
keyPeople.outcome: Executed in February 1929; the killing deepened the government’s hostility to militant Catholicism.

keyPeople.name: Leopoldo Ruiz y Flores
keyPeople.role: Archbishop of Morelia and apostolic delegate
keyPeople.focus: Negotiated the arreglos of June 1929 with President Portes Gil.
keyPeople.outcome: Exiled again in the 1930s; died in Morelia in 1941.

keyPeople.name: Pascual Díaz Barreto
keyPeople.role: Jesuit bishop of Tabasco, later Archbishop of Mexico
keyPeople.focus: A leading episcopal opponent of armed rebellion and co-negotiator of the peace.
keyPeople.outcome: Became Archbishop of Mexico in 1929; resented by many Cristeros as the architect of their demobilisation.

keyPeople.name: Dwight Morrow
keyPeople.focus: With Fr John J. Burke, mediated between the government and the bishops in 1928–29.
keyPeople.outcome: Later a US senator; the settlement is often called the Morrow arrangement.

casualties.note: Jean Meyer estimated around 90,000 combatant deaths — roughly 56,000 on the federal side and 30,000 or more Cristeros. Civilian deaths from reprisals, reconcentration, banditry and disease were not systematically recorded and some writers give much higher totals; these figures should be treated as approximate. Tens of thousands more were displaced or emigrated to the United States.

effects: The arreglos of 1929 created a modus vivendi in which the Church accepted the Constitution in practice and the state largely refrained from enforcing its harshest articles.
The war consolidated the post-revolutionary state; Calles founded the ruling National Revolutionary Party (PNR) in 1929.
Large-scale migration from western Mexico to the United States followed the fighting.
Rural regions such as Los Altos retained a strongly Catholic, anti-government identity for generations.
effectsOnChurch: The Mexican Church channelled lay energy into Catholic Action rather than armed or partisan politics.
The bishops’ settlement left a lasting rift between the hierarchy and many rural Catholics who felt abandoned.
Martyrs of the persecution, including Miguel Pro, Cristóbal Magallanes and José Sánchez del Río, became prominent Catholic saints, especially from the 1980s.
Constitutional recognition of the churches and diplomatic relations with the Holy See came only in 1992.
conflicts.legacy: Long ignored by official Mexican history, the Cristiada was recovered by Jean Meyer’s research in the 1970s and by later regional historians. It remains a reference point both for Catholics who see it as a struggle for religious liberty and for those who stress the violence on both sides; the 2012 film For Greater Glory brought it to a wider audience.

dissenters.name: Pascual Díaz Barreto and other bishops
dissenters.text: A significant part of the episcopate refused to bless armed rebellion, arguing that it was neither likely to succeed nor justified, and worked instead for a negotiated settlement.

dissenters.name: Anacleto González Flores (before 1927)
dissenters.text: For years he preached Gandhi-like civil resistance — boycott, petition and passive non-compliance — warning that violence would bring disaster; he accepted the armed rising only after the Liga had launched it.

dissenters.name: John J. Burke
dissenters.text: The American Paulist priest worked quietly with Ambassador Morrow to bring bishops and government to the table, preferring an imperfect peace to continued bloodshed.

theatres.name: Sahuayo, Michoacán (killing of José Sánchez del Río)
Cerro del Cubilete (Cristo Rey monument dynamited)

campaigns.title: The Cristero campaign in Los Altos, 1929
campaigns.people: Cristero forces under Enrique Gorostieta, Fr Aristeo Pedroza and Fr José Reyes Vega (killed at Tepatitlán)
campaigns.text: In the highlands east of Guadalajara the Cristeros held the countryside, defeated a federal force at Tepatitlán on 19 April 1929 and moved between the ranches of Los Altos until Gorostieta was killed near Atotonilco on 2 June.

conflicts.name: The Spanish Civil War: “crusade” and anticlerical terror
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The war was fought over class, land, regional autonomy, the army’s place and the survival of a democratic republic, not over doctrine. But religion was one of its deepest fault lines. The Church was identified with the old order, and in the Republican zone revolutionary militias killed nearly 7,000 clergy and religious and burned thousands of churches in the summer of 1936. The insurgent Nationalists, in turn, adopted the language of ‘crusade’ with the blessing of most bishops, and Catholicism became the core of Franco’s ideology. Historians such as Paul Preston stress that the ‘crusade’ label legitimised a military rebellion and its own mass repression; others, such as Julius Ruiz and Mary Vincent, emphasise how far anticlerical violence was a deliberate revolutionary project. Religion was thus a major driver of mobilisation and violence on both sides, though rarely the original cause of the war.

sides.name: Republicans (Popular Front government, socialists, anarchists, communists, Basque and Catalan nationalists)
sides.faith: Largely secular or anticlerical; Basque nationalists were devoutly Catholic

conflicts.summary: The military rising of July 1936 against Spain’s Second Republic triggered a revolution and a three-year civil war. In the Republican zone nearly 7,000 priests, monks and nuns were murdered and churches burned; in the Nationalist zone, a far larger repression of perceived leftists was carried out under a cause that bishops proclaimed a ‘crusade’. Franco’s victory in 1939 created a National-Catholic dictatorship that lasted until 1975.
conflicts.story:
The Second Republic, proclaimed in April 1931, set out to break the power of the Church in a country where the Catholic religion had been the religion of the state. The 1931 Constitution separated Church and state, legalised divorce, ended state funding of clergy and, in Article 26, dissolved the Jesuits and barred religious orders from teaching; Manuel Azaña declared that ‘Spain has ceased to be Catholic’. In May 1931 crowds burned convents in Madrid, Málaga and other cities while authorities hesitated. Catholics organised politically in the CEDA, which won the 1933 elections, and the October 1934 revolution in Asturias saw some thirty-four priests and religious killed before the army, under Franco’s direction, crushed it brutally. The Popular Front’s narrow victory in February 1936 was followed by months of strikes, political murders and church burnings.

On 17–18 July 1936 army garrisons in Morocco and across Spain rose against the government. The coup failed in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and the Basque Country, splitting the country. Where it failed, the state’s authority collapsed into the hands of workers’ militias, and a revolutionary terror fell on landowners, right-wing politicians and above all the clergy. Between July and December 1936 thousands of priests, monks and nuns were shot — in Barbastro, Lleida, Toledo, Madrid and across Catalonia and Valencia — including the Bishop of Barbastro, Florentino Asensio, and 51 Claretian seminarians. Churches were burned, tombs desecrated and images destroyed; militiamen staged the ‘execution’ of the Sacred Heart monument at the Cerro de los Ángeles. The Republican government condemned much of this violence but could not control it until 1937.

In the Nationalist zone the repression was planned from the outset by the generals as a ‘cleansing’ of the left. Leftist politicians, union members, teachers, Freemasons and intellectuals, including the poet Federico García Lorca, were shot in their tens of thousands; at Badajoz in August 1936 the Army of Africa killed hundreds, perhaps thousands, after taking the city. Most bishops blessed the rising: Bishop Enrique Plá y Deniel’s pastoral letter ‘The Two Cities’ (September 1936) called it a ‘crusade’, and Cardinal Isidro Gomá of Toledo drafted the Collective Letter of the Spanish Bishops of 1 July 1937, which justified the war to the Catholic world. Yet the Nationalists also shot at least fourteen Basque priests in 1936 for supporting the Catholic Basque government, and the bombing of Guernica by the German Condor Legion on 26 April 1937 divided Catholic opinion abroad.

The war became an international struggle. Germany and Italy sent troops, aircraft and arms to Franco; the Soviet Union armed the Republic, and International Brigades of volunteers fought for it, while Britain and France pursued non-intervention. The Nationalists relieved the besieged Alcázar of Toledo in September 1936 but failed to take Madrid that winter; during the Madrid siege thousands of right-wing prisoners were massacred at Paracuellos de Jarama in November–December 1936. The Nationalists conquered the Basque Country and the north in 1937, cut the Republic in two in 1938, won the long battle of the Ebro (July–November 1938), took Barcelona in January 1939 and Madrid on 28 March; Franco declared the war over on 1 April 1939.

Victory brought a ‘peace’ of reprisals: perhaps 20,000 Republicans were executed after the war, hundreds of thousands passed through prisons and camps, and around half a million went into exile. The new regime restored the Church’s privileges, its control of education and its moral authority, a system later called National Catholicism. The Concordat of 1953 sealed the alliance. Pope Pius XI had in September 1936 blessed the defenders of religion while also asking them to love their enemies; Pius XII congratulated Franco on his victory in 1939.

From the 1960s, under the influence of the Second Vatican Council, many Spanish Catholics distanced themselves from the regime. In 1971 a Joint Assembly of bishops and priests debated a motion asking pardon for the Church’s failure to be a ministry of reconciliation in the war; it won a majority but not the two-thirds needed. Since 1987 the Catholic Church has beatified more than 2,000 victims of the 1936 persecution, including 498 in 2007 and 522 at Tarragona in 2013, while the Historical Memory Law of 2007 and the Democratic Memory Law of 2022 address the victims of Francoist repression, including the exhumation of Franco from the Valley of the Fallen in 2019.
conflicts.nameOfGod: The Nationalist cause was proclaimed a ‘Crusade’ (Cruzada) for God and Spain. Bishop Plá y Deniel’s ‘The Two Cities’ (1936) drew on Augustine to set the city of God against the city of the godless; the bishops’ Collective Letter of 1937 called the war an ‘armed plebiscite’ in defence of Christian civilisation. Requetés of the Carlist militia went into battle with the Sacred Heart badge and the cry ‘¡Viva Cristo Rey!’, chaplains accompanied Nationalist units, and Franco presented himself as ‘Caudillo by the grace of God’. On the Republican side, revolutionary anticlericalism attacked the Church as the ideological prop of oppression and sought to eradicate public religion altogether.
religiousCauses: The Church was closely identified with the monarchy, landowners and the right, and anticlericalism had deep roots among Spanish workers and peasants since the nineteenth century.
The Republic’s constitution and laws of 1931–33 dissolved the Jesuits, barred religious orders from teaching and secularised marriage and cemeteries, which Catholics saw as persecution.
Waves of church burnings in 1931, 1934 and 1936 convinced many Catholics that the Republic threatened religion itself.
Catholic political mobilisation through the CEDA and Catholic Action made religion a central axis of electoral conflict.
The bishops’ framing of the rising as a ‘crusade’ gave the Nationalist cause religious legitimacy at home and abroad.
otherCauses: Agrarian conflict between large landowners and landless labourers, especially in Andalusia and Extremadura.
Militant labour movements — anarchist, socialist and communist — and fears of revolution after Asturias in 1934.
Army officers’ hostility to military reforms and to Catalan and Basque autonomy.
The European polarisation between fascism and communism, and the intervention of Germany, Italy and the Soviet Union.
Political violence and the breakdown of public order in the spring of 1936.
triggers: The victory of the Popular Front in the elections of February 1936.
The murder of the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo by Republican police on 13 July 1936.
The military coup of 17–18 July 1936 and its partial failure.

timeline.text: Proclamation of the Second Republic (April); convent burnings (May); anticlerical Constitution (December).
The Society of Jesus is dissolved in Spain.
Revolution in Asturias; some thirty-four priests and religious killed; the army crushes the rising.
Popular Front victory (February); military coup (17–18 July); anticlerical killings across the Republican zone; massacre at Badajoz (August).
Plá y Deniel’s ‘The Two Cities’ calls the war a crusade (September); Alcázar of Toledo relieved; Paracuellos massacres (November–December).
Bombing of Guernica (26 April); Collective Letter of the Spanish bishops (1 July); fall of Bilbao and the north.
Battle of the Ebro (July–November), the war’s largest battle.
Fall of Barcelona (January) and Madrid (28 March); Franco declares victory on 1 April; Pius XII congratulates him.
Concordat between Franco’s Spain and the Holy See.
Joint Assembly of bishops and priests debates asking pardon for the Church’s role in the war.
Beatification of 498 martyrs of 1934–37 and passage of the Historical Memory Law.
Beatification of 522 martyrs at Tarragona.

keyPeople.name: Francisco Franco
keyPeople.role: Nationalist commander and head of state
keyPeople.focus: Led the Army of Africa, became Generalísimo in 1936 and directed the war and its repression.
keyPeople.outcome: Ruled Spain as dictator until his death in 1975; buried at the Valley of the Fallen until exhumed in 2019.

keyPeople.name: Isidro Gomá y Tomás
keyPeople.role: Cardinal Archbishop of Toledo and Primate of Spain
keyPeople.focus: Acted as the Nationalists’ informal representative to the Vatican and drafted the bishops’ Collective Letter of 1937.
keyPeople.outcome: Later clashed with the regime over Nazi influence; died in 1940.

keyPeople.name: Enrique Plá y Deniel
keyPeople.role: Bishop of Salamanca, later Archbishop of Toledo
keyPeople.focus: His pastoral letter ‘The Two Cities’ (1936) gave the rising its theology of crusade; he lent Franco his palace as headquarters.
keyPeople.outcome: Primate of Spain 1941–68, a pillar of National Catholicism.

keyPeople.name: Francesc Vidal i Barraquer
keyPeople.focus: Rescued from the anarchists in 1936 by the Catalan government, he refused to sign the 1937 Collective Letter and worked for mediation.
keyPeople.outcome: Franco barred his return to Spain; he died in exile in Switzerland in 1943.

keyPeople.name: Mateo Múgica
keyPeople.focus: Expelled by the Nationalists, he protested to the Pope against their execution of Basque priests and did not sign the Collective Letter.
keyPeople.outcome: Returned to Spain in 1947 but never to his diocese.

keyPeople.name: Florentino Asensio Barroso
keyPeople.focus: Arrested by anarchist militias, tortured and shot in August 1936.
keyPeople.outcome: Beatified in 1997 as one of the martyrs of the persecution.

keyPeople.name: Manuel Azaña
keyPeople.role: Prime minister and President of the Republic
keyPeople.focus: Architect of the 1931 religious laws; as president during the war he deplored the terror and in 1938 appealed for ‘peace, pity and pardon’.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in exile in France in 1940.

keyPeople.name: Georges Bernanos
keyPeople.focus: Witnessed the Nationalist repression on Majorca and denounced it in Les Grands Cimetières sous la lune (1938).
keyPeople.outcome: Broke with the Catholic right; his book became a landmark of Catholic dissent.

casualties.note: Total deaths from combat, repression and war-related causes are usually estimated at 350,000–500,000. Antonio Montero Moreno’s count of the anticlerical violence (1961) — 13 bishops, 4,184 diocesan priests and seminarians, 2,365 male religious and 283 nuns, some 6,832 in all — is widely accepted. Paul Preston and others estimate around 50,000 killed in the Republican zone’s repression and about 130,000 in Nationalist repression during the war, plus perhaps 20,000 executions after 1939; these repression figures remain debated as local research continues.

effects: Franco’s dictatorship ruled Spain until 1975, with political parties banned and regional languages suppressed.
Around half a million Spaniards went into exile in 1939, many to France and Mexico.
The war served as a proving ground for German and Italian air power and tactics before the Second World War.
The memory of the war — exhumations, monuments and the Valley of the Fallen — remains politically divisive in Spain.
effectsOnChurch: The Church regained privileges, control of education and moral censorship under National Catholicism, sealed in the 1953 Concordat.
The killing of nearly 7,000 clergy and religious left a lasting memory of martyrdom, expressed in more than 2,000 beatifications since 1987.
The Church’s identification with the victors alienated many Spaniards and contributed to rapid secularisation after 1975.

From the 1960s Catholic workers’ movements, Basque and Catalan clergy and bishops such as Cardinal Vicente Enrique y Tarancón distanced the Church from the regime and supported the transition to democracy.
conflicts.legacy: The Spanish Civil War is a classic case of mutual sacralisation: one side making war on religion and the other making war in its name. Catholic opinion abroad split — Bernanos, Maritain and Mounier against the ‘crusade’, many others for it — and the Church in Spain has since struggled to honour its martyrs without appearing to forget the victims of the side it blessed.

dissenters.name: Francesc Vidal i Barraquer
dissenters.text: The Archbishop of Tarragona refused to sign the bishops’ Collective Letter of 1937 and pressed the Vatican to promote a negotiated peace and protect civilians on both sides.

dissenters.name: Mateo Múgica
dissenters.text: The Bishop of Vitoria protested to Rome against the Nationalists’ execution of Basque priests and refused to endorse the crusade.

dissenters.name: Georges Bernanos
dissenters.text: The French Catholic novelist, initially sympathetic to the rising, exposed the Nationalist killings on Majorca and the clergy who condoned them.

dissenters.name: Jacques Maritain
dissenters.text: The Catholic philosopher rejected the description of the war as a holy war, arguing in 1937 that it was a sacrilege to call it a holy war and to kill in the name of God.

dissenters.name: Basque Catholic clergy
dissenters.text: Many Basque priests supported the Republic’s Catholic Basque government against Franco, and some, such as those shot in 1936, paid with their lives.

Salamanca (Nationalist headquarters in the bishop’s palace)

campaigns.title: The Army of Africa’s march on Madrid
campaigns.people: Moroccan Regulares and the Spanish Legion under Franco, Juan Yagüe and José Varela
campaigns.text: Airlifted across the Strait from July 1936, the colonial army advanced from Seville through Extremadura, massacring prisoners at Badajoz, diverted to relieve the Alcázar of Toledo in September and reached the outskirts of Madrid in November, where its assault was halted.

campaigns.title: The Nationalist campaign in the north
campaigns.people: Nationalist armies under Emilio Mola and later Fidel Dávila, with the German Condor Legion and Italian troops
campaigns.text: From March 1937 the Nationalists attacked the Catholic Basque Country — bombing Durango and Guernica — took Bilbao in June, Santander in August and Asturias by October, ending the Republic’s northern front.

conflicts.name: The Troubles in Northern Ireland
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The Troubles were not a theological war: the main republican and loyalist paramilitaries fought over national allegiance — a united Ireland or union with Britain — and over civil rights, policing and power. But the communities in conflict were defined by religion, ‘Protestant’ and ‘Catholic’ served as ethnic labels, and much killing was simply sectarian, targeting victims for their presumed religion. Historians and sociologists disagree on how much faith itself mattered: John Whyte and John McGarry and Brendan O’Leary treat the conflict as essentially ethno-national, while Steve Bruce argues that evangelical Protestantism, exemplified by Ian Paisley, was central to unionist identity and resistance. Most observers agree that religion was a contributing marker and reinforcer of division — and that churches were also important agents of peace.

sides.name: Republicans and nationalists (Provisional IRA, INLA; constitutional nationalists of the SDLP)
sides.faith: Overwhelmingly from Catholic communities; paramilitaries largely secular-nationalist

sides.name: Loyalists and unionists (UVF, UDA/UFF; Ulster Unionist and Democratic Unionist parties)
sides.faith: Overwhelmingly from Protestant communities: Presbyterian, Church of Ireland, Methodist, Free Presbyterian

sides.name: British state (Army, Royal Ulster Constabulary, Ulster Defence Regiment)
sides.faith: Secular state with an established Protestant monarchy
leaders: Successive British prime ministers from Harold Wilson to Tony Blair
Secretaries of State for Northern Ireland

conflicts.summary: Three decades of violence in Northern Ireland from 1968 to 1998 pitted republican paramilitaries seeking a united Ireland against loyalist paramilitaries and the British state, with communities divided along Catholic and Protestant lines. About 3,500 people were killed. Clergy were among the loudest voices both of sectarian division and of reconciliation, and church figures helped open the channels that led to the ceasefires of 1994 and the Good Friday Agreement of 1998.
conflicts.story:
The division of Ulster into Protestant and Catholic communities went back to the Plantation of the early seventeenth century and the wars of the 1640s and 1690s. When Ireland was partitioned in 1921, Northern Ireland was created with a Protestant and unionist majority of about two-thirds; its first prime minister spoke of ‘a Protestant parliament and a Protestant state’. Catholics, largely nationalist, faced discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting, and the mostly Protestant police, including the auxiliary B-Specials, were distrusted. Separate churches, schools, sports and marching traditions — the Orange Order’s parades on the Twelfth of July above all — kept the communities apart.

In the late 1960s a civil rights movement, led by the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association and People’s Democracy, demanded ‘one man, one vote’ and fair housing. The police attack on a march in Derry on 5 October 1968 and a loyalist ambush of marchers at Burntollet Bridge in January 1969 radicalised the movement, while the Free Presbyterian preacher Ian Paisley mobilised Protestant fears that civil rights was a front for republicanism and ‘Romanism’. In August 1969 the ‘Battle of the Bogside’ in Derry and riots in Belfast, where Catholic streets were burned, led the British government to deploy troops on 14 August. The IRA split, and the new Provisional IRA began a campaign to drive Britain out.

The early 1970s were the most violent years. Internment without trial, introduced in August 1971, fell almost entirely on Catholics. On Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, British paratroopers shot dead thirteen unarmed civil rights marchers in Derry (a fourteenth died later); in July the IRA’s ‘Bloody Friday’ bombs killed nine in Belfast. Stormont was suspended and direct rule from London imposed. Loyalist paramilitaries — the Ulster Volunteer Force, whose motto was ‘For God and Ulster’, and the Ulster Defence Association — murdered hundreds of Catholic civilians, sometimes with torture, as by the ‘Shankill Butchers’. The power-sharing Sunningdale settlement collapsed in May 1974 under a loyalist workers’ strike, the same month loyalist bombs killed 34 people in Dublin and Monaghan.

Violence became more entrenched. The IRA bombed English cities, including Birmingham in 1974; at Kingsmill in 1976 republicans singled out and shot ten Protestant workmen; in 1983 gunmen of an INLA splinter group fired on a Pentecostal congregation at Darkley, killing three elders. The 1981 hunger strikes, in which Bobby Sands and nine others died, brought Sinn Féin into electoral politics. The Anglo-Irish Agreement of 1985, giving Dublin a consultative role, was met by Paisley’s ‘Ulster says No’. On Remembrance Sunday 1987 an IRA bomb at Enniskillen killed eleven people; Gordon Wilson, a Methodist whose daughter Marie died holding his hand, publicly forgave the bombers and pleaded that there be no retaliation.

Behind the scenes, clergy built bridges. Fr Alec Reid, a Redemptorist at Clonard Monastery in west Belfast, carried messages between Gerry Adams and the SDLP leader John Hume and between republicans and the Irish government from the late 1980s; in March 1988 he was photographed kneeling over two British corporals killed by an IRA crowd, having tried to save them. Presbyterian and Methodist ministers, such as Ken Newell and the Clonard–Fitzroy fellowship, and the Corrymeela Community founded by Ray Davey in 1965, sustained cross-community contact. Protestant clergy had met the IRA at Feakle in December 1974, and the Presbyterian minister Roy Magee helped persuade loyalist paramilitaries to call their ceasefire.

The Hume–Adams dialogue and the Downing Street Declaration of December 1993 led to the IRA ceasefire of 31 August 1994 and the loyalist ceasefire of 13 October. The IRA broke its ceasefire with the Canary Wharf bomb in February 1996 but renewed it in July 1997, while the stand-off over the Orange parade at Drumcree church in Portadown brought annual crises in 1995–98. Negotiations chaired by the US senator George Mitchell produced the Belfast or Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998, endorsed by referendums north and south. Four months later a ‘Real IRA’ bomb at Omagh killed 29 people, the deadliest single attack of the Troubles.

Power-sharing proved fragile, but the IRA decommissioned its weapons in 2005, witnessed by the Methodist former president Harold Good and the Catholic priest Alec Reid. In 2007 Ian Paisley, once the most uncompromising voice of Protestant resistance, became First Minister alongside Martin McGuinness of Sinn Féin. ‘Peace walls’ still divide parts of Belfast, and the legacy of unsolved killings, collusion between security forces and loyalists, and the treatment of victims remain painfully contested.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Loyalism drew on a Protestant tradition in which Ulster’s Britishness was bound up with the Reformation, the 1690 victory of William of Orange and the Ulster Covenant of 1912; the UVF’s motto was ‘For God and Ulster’, Orange lodges marched with Bibles and banners, and Paisley denounced the papacy and ecumenism alike. Republicans rarely invoked God directly, but drew on the Catholic imagery of martyrdom and sacrifice, especially around the 1981 hunger strikes, and Catholic funeral rites became occasions of mass republican mobilisation. All the main church leaders repeatedly condemned paramilitary violence as incompatible with Christianity.
religiousCauses: Protestant and Catholic identities had for centuries coincided with settler and native, unionist and nationalist allegiances, so religion served as the boundary between communities.
Evangelical anti-Catholicism, expressed by Ian Paisley and the Free Presbyterian Church, framed a united Ireland as subjection to Rome (‘Home Rule is Rome Rule’).
Separate church-run schools and the Catholic Church’s rules on mixed marriages reinforced segregation.
The Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, linked religion to unionist politics and annual marches that triggered confrontations.
The Irish Free State and Republic’s Catholic ethos, including the special position of the Catholic Church in the 1937 Constitution, deepened Protestant fears.
otherCauses: Partition in 1921 left a nationalist minority inside a state many of them regarded as illegitimate.
Systematic discrimination in housing, employment and local-government franchise, including gerrymandering in Derry.
A mainly Protestant police and the B-Specials, and later the security forces’ tactics, were seen as partisan by Catholics.
Economic decline in shipbuilding and linen and high unemployment, especially in working-class districts on both sides.
The republican tradition of armed struggle dating back to the Fenians and 1916, and the loyalist tradition of armed resistance from the 1912 Ulster Volunteers.
triggers: The police attack on the civil rights march in Derry on 5 October 1968.
The Burntollet ambush of January 1969 and the riots of August 1969, followed by the deployment of British troops.
Internment without trial in August 1971 and Bloody Sunday on 30 January 1972.

timeline.text: Police baton civil rights marchers in Derry on 5 October.
Burntollet ambush (January); Battle of the Bogside and Belfast riots; British troops deployed (14 August); IRA splits.
Internment without trial introduced; Paisley founds the Democratic Unionist Party.
Bloody Sunday in Derry (30 January); direct rule from London; Bloody Friday in Belfast — the deadliest year, with about 480 killed.
Sunningdale power-sharing collapses; Dublin and Monaghan bombings; Birmingham pub bombings; Protestant churchmen meet the IRA at Feakle.
Pope John Paul II at Drogheda pleads ‘on my knees’ for an end to violence.
Hunger strikes in the Maze prison; Bobby Sands and nine others die.
Gunmen attack the Mountain Lodge Pentecostal church at Darkley, killing three.
IRA bomb at the Enniskillen Remembrance Day ceremony kills eleven; Gordon Wilson forgives.
Shankill Road bomb and Greysteel massacre; Downing Street Declaration.
IRA ceasefire (31 August) and loyalist ceasefire (13 October).
Good Friday Agreement (10 April); Omagh bombing (15 August) kills 29.
IRA decommissioning witnessed by Fr Alec Reid and Rev Harold Good.
Ian Paisley and Martin McGuinness become First and Deputy First Ministers.

keyPeople.name: Ian Paisley
keyPeople.role: Founder of the Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster and the Democratic Unionist Party
keyPeople.focus: Mobilised Protestant opposition to civil rights, ecumenism, power-sharing and the Anglo-Irish Agreement with fiercely anti-Catholic preaching.
keyPeople.outcome: Agreed to share power with Sinn Féin and served as First Minister in 2007–08; created Baron Bannside.

keyPeople.name: John Hume
keyPeople.role: Leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party
keyPeople.focus: Champion of non-violent nationalism whose dialogue with Gerry Adams helped bring the IRA into politics.
keyPeople.outcome: Shared the 1998 Nobel Peace Prize with David Trimble.

keyPeople.name: Gerry Adams
keyPeople.focus: Led the republican movement’s shift from armed struggle to politics through secret talks and the peace process.
keyPeople.outcome: Long accused of IRA leadership, which he denied; stepped down as Sinn Féin president in 2018.

keyPeople.name: Alec Reid
keyPeople.role: Redemptorist priest at Clonard Monastery, Belfast
keyPeople.focus: Opened the secret channels between Adams, Hume and the Irish government that underlay the peace process.
keyPeople.outcome: Witnessed IRA decommissioning in 2005; widely honoured as a peacemaker.

keyPeople.name: Cahal Daly
keyPeople.role: Bishop of Down and Connor, then Cardinal Archbishop of Armagh
keyPeople.focus: Persistently condemned IRA violence as unjustifiable and promoted inter-church dialogue.
keyPeople.outcome: Cardinal from 1991; regarded as a voice of moral clarity against paramilitarism.

keyPeople.name: Bobby Sands
keyPeople.focus: Led the 1981 hunger strike for political status and was elected MP for Fermanagh and South Tyrone during it.
keyPeople.outcome: Died on 5 May 1981; became a republican icon.

keyPeople.name: Gordon Wilson
keyPeople.focus: Publicly forgave the IRA bombers who killed his daughter Marie in 1987 and later met the IRA to plead for peace.
keyPeople.outcome: Served in the Irish Senate; his words are credited with averting loyalist retaliation.

keyPeople.name: David Trimble
keyPeople.role: Leader of the Ulster Unionist Party
keyPeople.focus: Negotiated and sold the Good Friday Agreement to unionists.
keyPeople.outcome: First First Minister of Northern Ireland and Nobel laureate in 1998.

keyPeople.name: Martin McGuinness
keyPeople.role: IRA commander and Sinn Féin negotiator
keyPeople.focus: Moved from leadership of the IRA in Derry to chief republican negotiator.
keyPeople.outcome: Deputy First Minister 2007–17, forming an unexpected friendship with Paisley.

casualties.note: Malcolm Sutton’s index (CAIN, Ulster University) records about 3,530 deaths from 1969 to 2001; Lost Lives (McKittrick et al.) counts about 3,720 by 2006, including later deaths. Republican paramilitaries were responsible for roughly 60 per cent, loyalists for about 30 per cent and the security forces for about 10 per cent. Over half of those killed were civilians, and some 47,000 people were injured.

effects: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 established power-sharing government, cross-border bodies and the principle of consent for any change in constitutional status.
Political violence fell dramatically, though dissident republican attacks and punishment beatings persisted.
Residential and educational segregation deepened during the conflict, and ‘peace walls’ still stand in Belfast.
Inquiries such as the Saville Inquiry into Bloody Sunday (2010) and continuing disputes over legacy prosecutions keep the past politically live.
effectsOnChurch: Church leaders’ joint statements and cross-community initiatives, such as Corrymeela, Clonard–Fitzroy and the Irish Inter-Church Meeting, helped build the climate for peace.
Clergy such as Alec Reid, Harold Good and Roy Magee played direct roles as intermediaries with paramilitaries.
Religious practice declined sharply after the conflict, partly as churches were associated with sectarian division and, in the Catholic case, abuse scandals.
Evangelical unionism, represented by Paisley’s Free Presbyterian Church, moved from rejection to participation in power-sharing.
conflicts.legacy: The Troubles are often cited as a ‘religious war’, but most scholars describe an ethno-national conflict in which religion defined the communities and sometimes sharpened hatred, while also supplying many of those who worked for peace. The peace process is studied worldwide as a case of church-assisted conflict resolution.

dissenters.name: Pope John Paul II at Drogheda
dissenters.text: On 29 September 1979 he told a crowd of about 300,000: ‘On my knees I beg you to turn away from the paths of violence’, insisting that violence was not the Christian way.

dissenters.name: Alec Reid
dissenters.text: The Redemptorist priest spent years in secret mediation, arguing that the Church must talk to men of violence to bring them to politics.

dissenters.name: Cahal Daly
dissenters.text: As bishop and cardinal he repeatedly denied that republican violence could meet any criterion of a just war and urged Catholics to reject it.

dissenters.name: Gordon Wilson
dissenters.text: After the Enniskillen bombing he said he bore the bombers no ill will and would pray for them, and urged that no one avenge his daughter.

dissenters.name: Ray Davey and the Corrymeela Community
dissenters.text: The Presbyterian chaplain founded a centre at Ballycastle in 1965 where Protestants and Catholics met throughout the Troubles.

dissenters.name: Harold Good and Ken Newell
dissenters.text: Methodist and Presbyterian ministers who built cross-community friendships with Catholic clergy and with republicans, and witnessed decommissioning.
