West Belfast (Falls and Shankill, Clonard Monastery)

campaigns.title: The People’s Democracy march, Belfast to Derry
campaigns.people: About 80 students and civil rights marchers of People’s Democracy, including Bernadette Devlin and Michael Farrell
campaigns.text: Modelled on the Selma–Montgomery march, the four-day march set out on 1 January 1969, was harassed along the route and on 4 January was ambushed at Burntollet Bridge by loyalists, including off-duty B-Specials, while police stood by; the violence radicalised Catholic opinion.

conflicts.name: The Lebanese Civil War
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Lebanon’s political system allocated power by religious community, and its militias were overwhelmingly confessional — Maronite Christian, Sunni, Shi‘a and Druze — so the war is often described as Christian against Muslim. Most historians, however, including Theodor Hanf, Kamal Salibi and Fawwaz Traboulsi, stress that confession functioned as political community rather than theology: the conflict concerned the distribution of power, the armed Palestinian presence, class inequality and the interventions of Syria, Israel, Iran and others. Alliances crossed religious lines — Christians fought Christians in 1978 and 1988–90, and Shi‘a Amal fought Palestinians and Hezbollah — and some Christian clergy and Maronite monastic orders openly supported the Christian militias, while others worked for reconciliation. Religion was a contributing marker and mobiliser rather than the cause.

sides.name: Lebanese Front and Christian militias (Kataeb/Phalange, Lebanese Forces, National Liberal Party’s Tigers, Guardians of the Cedars; later Michel Aoun’s army units)
sides.faith: Mainly Maronite Catholic, with other Christians

sides.name: Lebanese National Movement and Palestinian organisations (PLO, leftist and Arab nationalist parties)
sides.faith: Mainly Sunni, Druze and secular leftist, with some Christian and Shi‘a members

sides.name: Foreign powers (Syria, Israel and its proxy South Lebanon Army, the Multinational Force)
sides.faith: Various; interests strategic rather than religious

conflicts.summary: From 1975 to 1990 Lebanon’s confessional political system collapsed into a war of militias divided largely by religious community, entangled with the Palestinian, Syrian, Israeli and Iranian struggles in the region. Massacres were committed by all sides — Karantina, Damour, Tel al-Zaatar, Sabra and Shatila, the Chouf. The Taif Agreement of 1989 ended the war by reapportioning power between Christians and Muslims, leaving Syria dominant until 2005.
conflicts.story:
Modern Lebanon was built on a balance between religious communities. Mount Lebanon’s Maronite Christians had enjoyed autonomy under the Ottomans after the Druze–Christian massacres of 1860, and the French mandate created Greater Lebanon in 1920 with a slim Christian majority. The unwritten National Pact of 1943 gave the presidency to a Maronite, the premiership to a Sunni and the speakership to a Shi‘a, and fixed parliamentary seats at six Christians to five Muslims, based on the census of 1932, the last ever held. By the 1970s Muslims, especially the poorer Shi‘a of the south and the Beirut suburbs, were a majority, and they and the left demanded reform that the Maronite establishment resisted.

The Palestinian presence upset the balance. Refugees from 1948 lived in camps, and after the PLO was expelled from Jordan in 1970–71 its fighters made Lebanon their base; the 1969 Cairo Agreement gave them autonomy in the camps. Many Christians saw an armed ‘state within the state’, while the Sunni, Druze and leftist Lebanese National Movement under Kamal Jumblatt saw the Palestinians as allies. Israeli reprisals against PLO raids fell on southern Lebanon. Both sides armed militias in the early 1970s.

On 13 April 1975 gunmen fired on the Phalangist leader Pierre Gemayel outside a church in Ain el-Remmaneh, killing several people; hours later Phalangists ambushed a bus carrying Palestinians, killing about two dozen. Fighting spread through Beirut, divided along the ‘Green Line’ into a Christian east and a Muslim west. Killings at checkpoints on the basis of religion recorded on identity cards became common — on ‘Black Saturday’, 6 December 1975, Phalangists killed scores of Muslims. In January 1976 Christian militias overran the Karantina slum, killing hundreds, and Palestinian and leftist forces sacked the Christian town of Damour, killing hundreds of civilians. In August 1976 the Christian militias took the Tel al-Zaatar refugee camp after a long siege, followed by massacres. Syria intervened in June 1976 — at first on the Christian side — and its Arab Deterrent Force stayed. Kamal Jumblatt was assassinated in March 1977, after which Druze killed many Christian villagers in the Chouf.

The war fractured further. In 1978 Bashir Gemayel’s forces killed his rival Tony Frangieh and his family at Ehden, and turned against the Syrians; Israel invaded the south in 1978 and set up a proxy militia. The Shi‘a cleric Musa al-Sadr, founder of Amal, vanished in Libya in 1978, and after the Iranian revolution Shi‘a militancy grew. In June 1982 Israel invaded to destroy the PLO, besieged West Beirut and secured the PLO’s evacuation by sea. Bashir Gemayel was elected president but was assassinated on 14 September 1982; between 16 and 18 September Lebanese Forces militiamen, in areas controlled by the Israeli army, massacred hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in the Sabra and Shatila camps. The Israeli Kahan Commission found Defence Minister Ariel Sharon indirectly responsible.

After Israel withdrew from the Chouf in 1983 the ‘Mountain War’ between the Druze and the Lebanese Forces led to massacres and the flight of tens of thousands of Christians from villages where they had lived beside Druze for centuries. Suicide bombings destroyed the US embassy and, on 23 October 1983, the US Marine and French barracks, killing 241 Americans and 58 French soldiers; the new Iranian-backed Hezbollah emerged and seized Western hostages. Amal fought the Palestinians in the ‘War of the Camps’ (1985–88) and then Hezbollah. In 1988 parliament failed to elect a president, and Michel Aoun, the army commander, headed a rival military government; his 1989 ‘war of liberation’ against Syria and his 1990 ‘war of elimination’ against Samir Geagea’s Lebanese Forces devastated the Christian heartland.

In October 1989 Lebanese deputies meeting at Taif in Saudi Arabia agreed to a new settlement: equal Christian and Muslim representation in parliament, a transfer of executive power from the Maronite president to the Sunni-led cabinet, the disarming of militias and recognition of Syria’s special role. The Maronite Patriarch Nasrallah Boutros Sfeir backed the accord against Aoun’s opposition. On 13 October 1990 Syrian forces attacked the presidential palace at Baabda and Aoun fled to the French embassy. An amnesty law of 1991 pardoned most wartime crimes; the militias, except Hezbollah, disarmed.

The war left perhaps 120,000–150,000 dead, around 17,000 missing and up to a million people displaced. Christian emigration accelerated, reducing their share of the population. Syria occupied Lebanon until 2005, Israel the south until 2000, and the confessional system, confirmed rather than abolished, continues to shape Lebanese politics. Pope John Paul II called Lebanon ‘more than a country: it is a message of freedom and an example of pluralism’ in 1989, convened a Special Synod for Lebanon in 1995 and visited in 1997.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Christian militias wore crosses and images of saints and the Virgin, and some presented their cause as the survival of the last free Christian homeland in the Middle East; the Lebanese Maronite Order of monks, under its superior Fr Charbel Kassis, gave money, land and fighters to the Lebanese Front, and the Kaslik monks’ university supported its ideology. On the Muslim side, Islamist movements, especially Hezbollah from 1982, framed the struggle against Israel and the West as jihad. Leaders on all sides, however, usually spoke the language of nation, community and survival rather than of holy war.
religiousCauses: The confessional political system of the 1943 National Pact tied power to religious community and froze it on the 1932 census.
Maronite fears of becoming a minority in a Muslim Arab world and of losing Lebanon’s character as a Christian refuge.
Muslim, especially Shi‘a, grievances at under-representation and deprivation in a system dominated by Christians and Sunni notables.
Memories of nineteenth-century Druze–Maronite massacres and communal fears of extermination.
The rise of political Islam after 1979, with Iran sponsoring Hezbollah.
otherCauses: The armed PLO presence after 1970 and Israeli reprisals turned Lebanon into a front of the Arab–Israeli conflict.
Severe social inequality between Beirut’s prosperous elites and the rural poor and slum dwellers.
A weak state and army, unable to control rival militias or the Palestinian organisations.
Intervention by Syria, Israel, Iran, Iraq, Libya and the Cold War superpowers, each backing local clients.
Rivalries between leading families and warlords within each community.
triggers: The attack on Pierre Gemayel at Ain el-Remmaneh and the Phalangist ambush of a Palestinian bus on 13 April 1975.
The breakdown of the army along confessional lines in early 1976.
The Syrian intervention of June 1976 and the Israeli invasions of 1978 and 1982.

timeline.text: The National Pact allocates power among religious communities at independence.
The Cairo Agreement recognises PLO autonomy in Lebanon’s refugee camps.
Ain el-Remmaneh bus massacre (13 April) begins the war; Black Saturday killings in Beirut (6 December).
Karantina and Damour massacres (January); Syrian intervention (June); fall of Tel al-Zaatar (August).
Kamal Jumblatt assassinated; reprisal killings of Christians in the Chouf.
Israel’s Litani operation; Ehden massacre; Musa al-Sadr disappears in Libya.
Israeli invasion and siege of West Beirut; PLO evacuation; Bashir Gemayel assassinated; Sabra and Shatila massacre (16–18 September).
Mountain War in the Chouf; bombings of the US embassy and the Multinational Force barracks.
Hezbollah publishes its Open Letter; War of the Camps begins.
Aoun’s war against Syria; John Paul II’s letter on Lebanon as a ‘message’; Taif Agreement (October).
Intra-Christian war between Aoun and the Lebanese Forces; Syrian assault ends Aoun’s government (13 October).
General amnesty law; militias other than Hezbollah disarm.
John Paul II visits Lebanon after the Special Synod for Lebanon.

keyPeople.name: Pierre Gemayel
keyPeople.focus: Led the largest Christian party and militia at the outbreak of war.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in 1984; his sons Bashir and Amin both became president.

keyPeople.name: Bashir Gemayel
keyPeople.focus: Unified the Christian militias by force and allied with Israel.
keyPeople.outcome: Elected president in August 1982 and assassinated on 14 September 1982 before taking office.

keyPeople.name: Kamal Jumblatt
keyPeople.role: Druze leader and head of the Lebanese National Movement
keyPeople.focus: Led the leftist–Muslim–Palestinian coalition demanding the end of confessional privilege.
keyPeople.outcome: Assassinated in March 1977, widely attributed to Syria.

keyPeople.name: Musa al-Sadr
keyPeople.role: Shi‘a cleric, founder of the Movement of the Deprived and Amal
keyPeople.focus: Mobilised the Shi‘a poor and sought dialogue with Christians, preaching in churches.
keyPeople.outcome: Disappeared on a visit to Libya in August 1978; his fate remains unknown.

keyPeople.name: Elie Hobeika
keyPeople.focus: Commanded the militiamen who carried out the Sabra and Shatila massacre.
keyPeople.outcome: Later a minister in post-war governments; killed by a car bomb in 2002.

keyPeople.name: Michel Aoun
keyPeople.role: Army commander and head of a rival military government 1988–90
keyPeople.focus: Fought Syria and the Lebanese Forces in the war’s last phase.
keyPeople.outcome: Exiled in France until 2005; President of Lebanon 2016–22.

keyPeople.name: Nasrallah Boutros Sfeir
keyPeople.focus: Supported the Taif Agreement and condemned intra-Christian fighting.
keyPeople.outcome: Later the leading Christian voice for Syrian withdrawal, achieved in 2005.

keyPeople.name: Yasser Arafat
keyPeople.focus: Led the Palestinian organisations based in Lebanon from 1970.
keyPeople.outcome: Evacuated from Beirut in August 1982; moved the PLO to Tunis.

casualties.note: Estimates of deaths from 1975 to 1990 usually range from about 120,000 to 150,000; a frequently cited count by Labaki and Abou Rjeily gives around 144,000. Some 17,000 people remain missing, and up to a million were displaced at some point. Because no census or official death registry was kept, all figures are approximate.

effects: The Taif Agreement of 1989 equalised Christian and Muslim parliamentary representation and shifted executive power to the Sunni prime minister and cabinet.
Syria dominated Lebanon until 2005 and Israel occupied the south until 2000.
Hezbollah emerged as the only armed militia to keep its weapons, becoming a dominant political and military force.
Mass emigration, especially of Christians, and the destruction of central Beirut transformed the country.
The 1991 amnesty and the absence of a truth process left wartime crimes and the missing unaddressed.
effectsOnChurch: Christian communities lost population and political primacy, with whole regions such as the Chouf emptied of Christians for years.
The involvement of some Maronite clergy and monks with militias provoked criticism within and beyond the Church.
The Maronite patriarchate under Sfeir became a national moral authority by backing Taif and later Lebanese sovereignty.
John Paul II’s Special Synod for Lebanon (1995) and apostolic exhortation A New Hope for Lebanon (1997) urged Christian–Muslim coexistence.
conflicts.legacy: The Lebanese war is a cautionary example of how a system designed to give religious communities security can turn them into armed political blocs. It also showed Christians as both perpetrators and victims, and produced voices — Christian and Muslim — who insisted that Lebanon’s plural society was worth preserving.

dissenters.name: Grégoire Haddad
dissenters.text: The Melkite archbishop of Beirut, known as the ‘red bishop’, called for a secular state and campaigned against confessionalism; he founded the Social Movement and was removed from his see in 1975 by his synod.

dissenters.name: Nasrallah Boutros Sfeir
dissenters.text: The Maronite Patriarch condemned the fratricidal Christian wars of 1988–90 and backed the Taif compromise despite fierce opposition from Aoun’s supporters.

dissenters.name: Pope John Paul II
dissenters.text: He made repeated appeals for peace, called for a day of prayer for Lebanon and in 1989 described Lebanon as a ‘message’ of coexistence for East and West.

dissenters.name: Georges Khodr
dissenters.text: The Greek Orthodox Metropolitan of Mount Lebanon wrote throughout the war against militia violence and for Christian–Muslim dialogue.

campaigns.title: Israel’s 1982 invasion and the siege of Beirut
campaigns.people: Israel Defense Forces under Defence Minister Ariel Sharon
campaigns.text: Launched on 6 June 1982, the invasion advanced up the coast, overrunning Palestinian camps around Tyre and Sidon, and besieged West Beirut for some ten weeks until the PLO agreed to evacuate in August; in September Israeli forces entered West Beirut, where the Sabra and Shatila massacre followed.

conflicts.name: The Yugoslav wars, Bosnia and Srebrenica
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The wars that destroyed Yugoslavia were driven by nationalist politicians, the collapse of communism and competing territorial projects. Because Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks speak essentially the same language, religion — Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim — was the main marker of national identity, and war aims of ‘ethnic cleansing’ were in practice religious cleansing: mosques, churches and monasteries were systematically destroyed and victims identified by their names and faith. Michael Sells argues that religious mythology, especially the Serbian Kosovo myth, was central to genocidal ideology (‘Christoslavism’); Vjekoslav Perica shows how churches became ‘national churches’ that sacralised nationalism; others, such as Laura Silber and Allan Little, emphasise political leaders who used religion instrumentally while being themselves ex-communists. The term ‘pretext’ fits the leaders; ‘contributing’ better fits the role of religious identity and clergy.

sides.name: Serbian forces (Yugoslav People’s Army, Army of Republika Srpska, Croatian Serb forces, paramilitaries such as Arkan’s Tigers and the Scorpions)
Croatian forces (Croatian Army, Croatian Defence Council in Bosnia)
Bosnian government and Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina
sides.faith: Mainly Bosniak Muslim, with Serb and Croat members, especially in Sarajevo and Tuzla

sides.name: International actors (UN Protection Force, NATO, European and US mediators)

conflicts.summary: As Yugoslavia disintegrated in 1991, wars in Slovenia, Croatia and then Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992–95) pitted Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks against one another in campaigns of ‘ethnic cleansing’ that targeted religious identity, culminating in the genocide of some 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in July 1995. Churches and religious leaders were drawn into national causes, sometimes blessing fighters, while others pleaded for peace. The Dayton Agreement of November 1995 ended the Bosnian war.
conflicts.story:
Yugoslavia contained Orthodox Serbs, Montenegrins and Macedonians, Catholic Croats and Slovenes, and Muslim Bosniaks and Albanians. The Second World War had left terrible memories: the Croatian Ustaša state, tolerated and in part supported by Catholic clergy, murdered hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews and Roma, notably at Jasenovac, and forcibly converted Serbs to Catholicism; Serbian Četniks massacred Muslims and Croats. Tito’s communist regime suppressed these memories under ‘brotherhood and unity’. After Tito’s death in 1980 and amid economic crisis, nationalists revived them. The Serbian Orthodox Church’s Kosovo myth — Prince Lazar’s choice of a heavenly kingdom at the battle of Kosovo in 1389 — was invoked as Lazar’s relics toured Serb lands in 1988–89, and on the 600th anniversary, 28 June 1989, Slobodan Milošević addressed a huge crowd at Gazimestan, warning that battles might again be fought.

In 1990 multi-party elections brought nationalists to power in the republics. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. After a ten-day war Slovenia was allowed to go, but in Croatia rebel Serbs, backed by the Yugoslav People’s Army, seized about a third of the country. Vukovar was besieged for three months and destroyed; after its fall on 18 November 1991 some 200 wounded and hospital staff were taken to the Ovčara farm and murdered. Dubrovnik was shelled. Croatian forces also expelled and killed Serb civilians, and the United Nations deployed peacekeepers in 1992.

Bosnia and Herzegovina, the most mixed republic, declared independence after a referendum boycotted by Serbs in early 1992. From April Bosnian Serb forces under Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić, with Serbian paramilitaries, seized some 70 per cent of the territory and ‘cleansed’ it of non-Serbs: towns such as Bijeljina, Zvornik, Foča, Višegrad and Prijedor saw mass killings, detention camps such as Omarska and Keraterm, and systematic rape. Mosques, Catholic churches and Ottoman monuments were deliberately destroyed, including the sixteenth-century Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka in May 1993; the National Library in Sarajevo was burned in August 1992. Sarajevo endured a siege from April 1992 to February 1996, in which over 11,000 people died, including the shelling of the Markale market in 1994 and 1995.

In 1993 a second war broke out between Bosnian Croats, backed by Tuđman’s Croatia, and the Bosniak-led government. Croat forces massacred Muslim villagers at Ahmići in April 1993 and destroyed Mostar’s Ottoman Old Bridge in November; the government army, joined by some foreign mujahideen, also committed abuses against Croat and Serb civilians. The Washington Agreement of March 1994 ended the Croat–Bosniak war. Meanwhile, UN ‘safe areas’ such as Srebrenica, Žepa and Goražde were left lightly defended.

In July 1995 Mladić’s forces overran Srebrenica. Dutch UN peacekeepers could not protect the population; women and children were bussed out, while around 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were captured and executed over a few days and buried in mass graves, many later moved to conceal them. Video later showed an Orthodox priest blessing members of the Scorpions unit before they shot six prisoners. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice later ruled the massacre genocide. In August 1995 Croatia’s Operation Storm retook the Krajina, causing some 150,000–200,000 Serbs to flee, with hundreds of civilians killed; NATO air strikes after the second Markale massacre and a Croat–Bosniak offensive brought the Serbs to the table.

The Dayton Agreement, negotiated in Ohio under Richard Holbrooke and signed in Paris on 14 December 1995, kept Bosnia as one state divided into a Bosniak–Croat Federation and Republika Srpska under a complex ethnic power-sharing system and international oversight. Karadžić and Mladić were later convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity at The Hague; Milošević died in 2006 during his trial. Conflict moved to Kosovo in 1998–99, ending after NATO’s bombing of Serbia, and to Macedonia in 2001.

The religious communities emerged as guardians of national identity in the new states. The Serbian Orthodox Church canonised some wartime figures and many of its hierarchs defended Karadžić; the Greek Orthodox Church even honoured him in 1993. The Catholic Church in Croatia, led by Cardinal Franjo Kuharić, called for respect for all victims but closely associated itself with the Croatian state. Islamic institutions became more central to Bosniak identity. At the same time interreligious councils, Franciscan friars of Bosnia, and individual Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim leaders worked for reconciliation, a task still unfinished in divided towns and contested memorials.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Serbian nationalists drew on the Kosovo covenant of Prince Lazar, the three-fingered Orthodox salute and the slogan ‘Only Unity Saves the Serbs’ (Samo sloga Srbina spasava) under the Orthodox cross; Orthodox priests blessed some units and paramilitaries, and Karadžić presented his cause as defending Christian Europe against an Islamic state. Croatian nationalism used the Catholic rosary, the cult of Cardinal Alojzije Stepinac and Our Lady of Medjugorje as identity symbols, and Croat units in Herzegovina bore Catholic insignia. Some Bosniak units adopted Islamic names and slogans, and foreign mujahideen fought as jihadists. Religious buildings of the enemy were targeted precisely because they signified the presence of the other people.
religiousCauses: Religion was the chief marker distinguishing Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks, who share a language, so national struggles became religious in form.
The Serbian Orthodox Kosovo myth and its revival around the 1989 anniversary sacralised Serbian nationalism and portrayed Muslims as betrayers of Christ.
Unresolved memories of the Second World War, including Ustaša forced conversions and massacres of Orthodox Serbs, and Četnik massacres of Muslims, fed mutual fear.
Churches that had suffered under communism embraced nationalist movements as partners in religious revival after 1989.
Propaganda portrayed Bosniaks as Islamic fundamentalists seeking a jihad state, and Croats and Serbs as crusaders, intensifying religious polarisation.
otherCauses: The economic crisis and debt of 1980s Yugoslavia and the end of communist legitimacy after 1989.
Ex-communist leaders, notably Milošević and Tuđman, used nationalism to win and keep power.
Competing territorial projects for a Greater Serbia and a Greater Croatia, including the 1991 Karađorđevo talks on partitioning Bosnia.
The Serb-dominated Yugoslav army’s control of weapons, and the arms embargo that disadvantaged the Bosnian government.
International hesitation and divided diplomacy that rewarded military faits accomplis.
triggers: The declarations of independence of Slovenia and Croatia on 25 June 1991.
The Bosnian independence referendum of February–March 1992 and international recognition in April 1992.
The Serb seizure of territory and siege of Sarajevo in April 1992.

timeline.text: Milošević addresses the 600th anniversary of the battle of Kosovo at Gazimestan (28 June).
Slovenia and Croatia declare independence (25 June); ten-day war in Slovenia; war in Croatia; fall of Vukovar and Ovčara massacre (November).
Bosnia declares independence; war begins in April; siege of Sarajevo; camps at Omarska and Keraterm; burning of Sarajevo’s National Library (August).
Croat–Bosniak war; Ahmići massacre (April); Ferhadija mosque destroyed (May); Stari Most in Mostar destroyed (November); ICTY established.
Markale market massacre (February); Washington Agreement ends the Croat–Bosniak war (March).
Srebrenica genocide (July); Operation Storm (August); NATO Operation Deliberate Force; Dayton Agreement (November–December).
Pope John Paul II visits Sarajevo (April).
War in Kosovo ends after NATO bombing of Serbia.
ICTY Appeals Chamber confirms the Srebrenica massacre as genocide in the Krstić case.
International Court of Justice rules Srebrenica genocide and finds Serbia failed to prevent it.
Final appeal confirms Ratko Mladić’s life sentence for genocide.

keyPeople.name: Slobodan Milošević
keyPeople.role: President of Serbia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
keyPeople.focus: Used Serbian nationalism and the Kosovo myth to rise to power and backed Serb forces in Croatia and Bosnia.
keyPeople.outcome: Extradited to The Hague in 2001; died in 2006 before his trial ended.

keyPeople.name: Franjo Tuđman
keyPeople.focus: Led Croatia to independence, sponsored the Bosnian Croat statelet of Herceg-Bosna and ordered Operation Storm.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in office in 1999; ICTY judgments later named him in a joint criminal enterprise in Bosnia.

keyPeople.name: Alija Izetbegović
keyPeople.focus: Led the Bosnian government through the war and signed Dayton; his earlier Islamic Declaration was used by opponents to portray him as a fundamentalist.
keyPeople.outcome: Retired in 2000; died in 2003.

keyPeople.name: Radovan Karadžić
keyPeople.focus: Directed the Bosnian Serb political leadership responsible for ethnic cleansing and the siege of Sarajevo, presenting himself as a defender of Orthodox Christianity.
keyPeople.outcome: Arrested in 2008; convicted of genocide at Srebrenica and sentenced to life imprisonment.

keyPeople.name: Ratko Mladić
keyPeople.role: Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska
keyPeople.focus: Commanded the siege of Sarajevo and the capture of Srebrenica.
keyPeople.outcome: Arrested in 2011; convicted of genocide and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2017, upheld in 2021.

keyPeople.name: Patriarch Pavle
keyPeople.role: Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church 1990–2009
keyPeople.focus: Defended Serb national claims but appealed repeatedly for peace and condemned crimes, saying that if a Greater Serbia could only be gained by crime he would not accept it.
keyPeople.outcome: Revered for personal asceticism; criticised for the church’s ties to Bosnian Serb leaders.

keyPeople.name: Vinko Puljić
keyPeople.role: Catholic Archbishop of Sarajevo, cardinal from 1994
keyPeople.focus: Remained in besieged Sarajevo and spoke for a united, multi-religious Bosnia.
keyPeople.outcome: Hosted John Paul II’s visit in 1997 and led the Catholic Church in Bosnia until 2022.

keyPeople.name: Franjo Kuharić
keyPeople.focus: Supported Croatian independence while urging Croats not to take revenge and to respect enemies’ lives and property.
keyPeople.outcome: Retired in 1997.

casualties.note: For Bosnia and Herzegovina the Research and Documentation Centre in Sarajevo (Bosnian Book of the Dead) identified about 97,000–100,000 killed, of whom roughly 40 per cent were civilians and most were Bosniaks; the ICTY demographic unit reached a similar figure. Deaths in the war in Croatia are estimated at about 20,000. Srebrenica alone accounted for some 8,000 victims. The range covers Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia in 1991–95; the Kosovo war of 1998–99 added about 13,000 further deaths. Over four million people were displaced.

effects: Yugoslavia was replaced by independent states, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided by Dayton into two ethnically defined entities under international supervision.
Ethnic cleansing largely succeeded: most towns became overwhelmingly mono-ethnic, and many refugees never returned.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (1993–2017) became a landmark of international criminal law, convicting leaders of all sides.
International failure at Srebrenica shaped the later doctrine of the ‘responsibility to protect’.
effectsOnChurch: The Serbian Orthodox and Croatian Catholic churches emerged as national institutions closely tied to their states, criticised for failing to confront crimes committed in their nations’ name.
Thousands of mosques, hundreds of Catholic churches and many Orthodox churches and monasteries were destroyed; their rebuilding, such as the Ferhadija mosque in 2016, became a test of reconciliation.
Interreligious councils, including the Inter-religious Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1997), were founded with Orthodox, Catholic, Muslim and Jewish leaders.
The Franciscans of Bosna Srebrena, who stayed with their communities and opposed partition, became an example of Catholic resistance to ethnic nationalism.
conflicts.legacy: The Bosnian war became the paradigm of ‘ethno-religious’ conflict in post-Cold War Europe and the occasion for Europe’s first genocide since the Holocaust. It raises hard questions for churches about the fusion of faith and nation, and about how clergy who blessed fighters or canonised nationalist heroes can contribute to truth and reconciliation.

dissenters.name: Pope John Paul II
dissenters.text: He repeatedly condemned ethnic cleansing, tried to visit besieged Sarajevo in 1994 and went there in April 1997, calling for forgiveness and reconciliation among all communities.

dissenters.name: Patriarch Pavle
dissenters.text: Despite his church’s nationalism, he declared that crimes committed in the name of the Serbian people could not be justified and that he would rather Serbia disappear than be built on crime.

dissenters.name: Franciscans of Bosna Srebrena
dissenters.text: Friars led by Fra Petar Anđelović and Fra Ivo Marković refused to support ethnic partition, stayed in mixed towns and later founded the interreligious choir Pontanima.

dissenters.name: Bishop Artemije of Raška and Prizren
dissenters.text: The Serbian Orthodox bishop of Kosovo openly opposed Milošević’s policies and condemned violence against both Albanians and Serbs.

dissenters.name: Cardinal Vinko Puljić
dissenters.text: He stayed in besieged Sarajevo, rejected the division of Bosnia into ethnic statelets and called on Catholics to protect their neighbours.

campaigns.title: The column from Srebrenica to Tuzla
campaigns.people: Some 10,000–15,000 Bosniak men and boys attempting to escape through the woods
campaigns.text: On the night of 11–12 July 1995 a column of men set out across Serb-held territory towards government lines; it was ambushed and shelled near Kamenica and the Konjević Polje–Nova Kasaba road, where thousands were captured and later executed. Survivors broke through at Baljkovica on 16 July and reached Tuzla. The route is retraced each year by the Marš mira peace march.

campaigns.title: Operation Storm
campaigns.people: Croatian Army under Generals Ante Gotovina and others
campaigns.text: On 4–7 August 1995 Croatian forces overran the self-declared Republic of Serbian Krajina, taking its capital Knin on 5 August. Most of the Serb population fled into Bosnia and Serbia, and the following weeks saw killings of elderly Serb civilians and widespread burning of homes.
